name: Atacama Desert (Yungay Core)
description: The hyperarid core of the Atacama is the driest non-polar desert on Earth, with some locations recording less than 1mm of rainfall per year. Salt-encrusted playas and iron-oxide coated rocks mirror the Martian surface chemistry.
why_analog: Soil perchlorate concentrations (0.01–0.5 wt%) and nitratine mineral assemblages match Phoenix and Curiosity lander discoveries on Mars. The extreme aridity (water activity aw < 0.15) and UV irradiance are the closest terrestrial approximation of Amazonian Mars conditions.

name: Haughton Impact Crater
description: A 23-km diameter complex impact crater formed ~23 million years ago in a polar desert. NASA's Haughton-Mars Project (HMP) has used it for decades to test Mars rovers, suits, and exploration protocols.
why_analog: Impact-shocked target rocks (carbonate/gneissic breccia), post-impact hydrothermal alteration producing clays and sulfates, and polygon-patterned permafrost ground match both the Moon's cratered highlands and Mars's Noachian terrains. Continuous permafrost serves as a cryosphere analog.

name: Death Valley (Badwater Basin)
description: The hottest and driest place in North America, featuring salt playas, desert pavements of ventifacted basalt pebbles, and maar volcanic craters — multiple Martian surface analogs in one location.
why_analog: Badwater Basin's evaporite sequence (halite, gypsum, borax) mirrors Martian paleolake deposits at Gale Crater. The 'Mars Hill' desert pavement with iron-oxide desert varnish matches Viking 1 and Pathfinder landing site imagery. Ubehebe Crater is a phreatomagmatic maar analog to Martian maar craters.

name: Devon Island (Polar Desert)
description: The world's largest uninhabited island — a vast Arctic polar desert with permafrost, polygon-patterned ground, and conditions closely mimicking early Mars and the lunar polar regions.
why_analog: Continuous deep permafrost (~500m), thermal contraction crack polygons (5–20m wavelength), and active layer dynamics are direct analogs to Martian high-latitude periglacial terrains at the Phoenix landing site (Vastitas Borealis).

name: Mauna Kea Lava Fields
description: The summit zone of Mauna Kea hosts ancient lava flows in a high-altitude, oxygen-thin environment. NASA uses these fields for lunar geology training and rover testing.
why_analog: Unweathered tholeiitic basalt lava composition (SiO₂ ~49–51%) closely matches lunar mare basalts. Lava tubes provide subsurface shelter analogs. Palagonite tephra's VIS-NIR spectral signature matches bright Martian dust. The sparse, rocky terrain mirrors Apollo landing sites.

name: Craters of the Moon (Lava Tubes)
description: A vast field of volcanic features including cinder cones, spatter cones, lava flows, and pit craters in Idaho — NASA trained Apollo astronauts here in the 1960s.
why_analog: The lava tube skylights and subsurface caves are analogs to Marius Hills pit craters on the Moon (proposed lunar base shelter sites). Spatter cones and aa lava fields match the rough lunar highland terrain. The site's remoteness and monochromatic basaltic landscape provide psychological isolation training too.

name: McMurdo Dry Valleys
description: One of the most extreme and Mars-like environments on Earth — ice-free valleys in Antarctica where liquid water is essentially absent and endolithic cyanobacteria are sheltered inside porous rocks.
why_analog: Water activity can drop below 0.10, the driest known terrestrial habitat. Sand wedge polygons and thermal contraction cracks directly mirror Martian high-latitude periglacial terrain. Cryptoendolithic life inside rocks provides the closest analog to potential subsurface Martian life.

name: Río Tinto Acid River
description: A river with pH 1.5–2.5 flowing through massive sulfide ore deposits. The red color comes from dissolved iron and iron-oxide precipitates — matching the Martian mineralogy of Meridiani Planum.
why_analog: The world's best analog for Martian acid-sulfate mineralogy. Jarosite [KFe₃(SO₄)₂(OH)₆], hematite 'blueberries', and goethite — the exact minerals identified by the Mars Opportunity rover at Meridiani Planum — form naturally here through iron sulfide oxidation.

name: Dallol Hydrothermal Field
description: The hottest inhabited place on Earth, with hyperacid brine pools (pH < 0), vivid sulfur deposits, and chloride/sulfate salt pans in the Danakil Depression — one of the most alien landscapes on Earth.
why_analog: Extreme brine chemistry (Cl/SO₄ dominated), sulfur-rich hydrothermal vents, and iron-oxide salt crusts match proposed early Mars hydrothermal environments. The hypersaline, highly acidic brines are among the few terrestrial analogs for proposed transient liquid water on present-day Mars.

name: Erta Ale Lava Lake
description: One of the world's few permanent lava lakes in a shield volcano — a glimpse of the active lunar surface during the mare basalt eruption period ~3.5 billion years ago.
why_analog: Active tholeiitic basalt lava eruptions with composition (SiO₂ ~48%, FeO ~12%) matching lunar mare basalt. Fresh lava flow surfaces provide direct analogs to young lunar mare terrain before space weathering. The shield volcano morphology also mirrors broad lunar volcanic structures.

name: Askja / Holuhraun (Iceland)
description: Iceland's volcanic highlands — used by Apollo astronauts for field geology training. Holuhraun (2014–15 eruption) created the largest basalt lava field in Iceland in 200 years.
why_analog: ESA trained astronauts here for lunar surface geology. Fresh basalt lava flows, caldera lakes, geothermal features, and palagonite tephra (spectrally identical to Martian bright dust) make Askja an exceptional dual-body analog. Apollo 11 crew trained in Iceland in 1965.

name: Namib Desert (Sossusvlei)
description: One of the world's oldest deserts (55–80 million years), featuring massive aeolian sand dunes — the largest on Earth — and dry salt pan depressions (vleis) analogous to Martian dry paleolakes.
why_analog: Giant aeolian dune systems mirror Martian sand seas (ergs) like the Bagnold Dunes explored by Curiosity. The dry clay pans (vleis) resemble ancient Martian lake bed deposits. Extreme aridity and high diurnal temperature swings add to the Martian parallel.

name: Tabernas Desert (Badlands)
description: Europe's only true semi-arid desert, with heavily eroded badlands, clay-rich soils, and a landscape that has hosted both film sets and Mars analog research.
why_analog: The clay-rich eroded badlands contain smectite and gypsum that closely match the mineralogy of Mars's Hesperian-age sedimentary deposits. ESA's ExoMars team uses Tabernas as a field site. The UV exposure is among Europe's highest.

name: Lanzarote Lava Fields (Timanfaya)
description: Lanzarote's volcanic badlands from the 1730–36 eruptions — ESA has trained astronauts here since 2011 in the CAVES and PANGAEA programs for underground and planetary geology.
why_analog: One of ESA's official astronaut training sites for Moon and Mars geology. The extensive lava tube network at Jameos del Agua provides direct analogs to lunar lava tube shelters. The recent (300-year-old) basaltic flows are essentially unweathered, mirroring young lunar mare surfaces.
target_region: Lacus Mortis / Marius Hills pit craters

name: Nördlingen Impact Crater
description: A 15-km diameter impact crater (Ries Crater) formed 14.6 million years ago in Germany. The city of Nördlingen sits inside it and its buildings are made of suevite impact breccia containing shocked minerals.
why_analog: The suevite breccia, shocked quartz PDFs (planar deformation features), diaplectic glass, and hydrothermal post-impact minerals provide a well-studied ground truth for impact processes on the Moon and Mars. Apollo astronauts trained at Ries Crater in 1970.

name: Qaidam Basin
description: A high-altitude Tibetan Plateau basin with Mars-like salt flats, evaporite deposits, and cold arid conditions. China's CNSA uses it as a Mars analog test site.
why_analog: The Qaidam Basin is recognized by CNSA and international researchers as one of the best Mars analogs in Asia — featuring salt-encrusted lake beds, sulfate-rich soils, extreme diurnal temperature variation, and strong UV at altitude. Surface albedo and spectral features closely match Mars imagery.

name: Kilauea Active Lava Flows
description: One of Earth's most active shield volcanoes, producing continuous tholeiitic basalt flows of both pāhoehoe (smooth) and 'a'ā (clinkery) morphologies — mirroring the full range of lunar and Martian volcanic terrains.
why_analog: Fresh basalt composition (SiO₂ ~49%, FeO ~12%) is the closest Earth match to lunar mare basalt and Martian basaltic plains. The pāhoehoe/ʻaʻā duality mirrors Lunar/Martian flow types. Hawaiian lava tubes (up to 30m wide) are ground-truth analogs for the proposed much larger Moon/Mars lava tube shelters.

name: Sahara Great Sand Seas (Ergs)
description: The world's largest hot desert and its erg systems — vast linear and star dune fields that mirror Martian sand seas observed by MRO from orbit.
why_analog: Mega-dune fields with star dunes, linear dunes, and interdune corridors mirror the Bagnold Dunes at Gale Crater and the north polar erg (Olympia Undae) on Mars. Extreme aridity, wind erosion (ventifacts), and high UV exposure complete the analogy.

name: Kamchatka Volcanoes
description: Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula hosts one of the densest concentrations of active volcanoes on Earth — 30 active volcanoes in an area the size of California — with varied tholeiitic basalt and geothermal features.
why_analog: Multiple concurrent active volcanoes in various stages of eruption, fumarolic activity, lava flow types (pāhoehoe to block lava), and geothermal features provide exceptional training ground for planetary volcanology. The sub-arctic volcanic setting mirrors hypothetical ancient lunar/Martian sub-glacial volcanism.
